title: Post-Operative Pulmonary Embolism: A Clinical Deep Dive
summary: Pulmonary Embolism (PE) is a life-threatening post-surgical complication characterized by the occlusion of the pulmonary arterial tree. This guide provides an evidence-based framework for the rapid diagnosis, risk stratification, and management of PE in the post-operative setting.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Pulmonary Embolism (PE) is the obstruction of one or more pulmonary arteries by solid, liquid, or gaseous masses. In the post-operative ophthalmic patient, the most common etiology is a dislodged Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) from the lower extremities. While ophthalmic procedures are often perceived as 'low risk,' prolonged immobility, general anesthesia, and underlying patient comorbidities (e.g., malignancy, Factor V Leiden) can precipitate a fatal embolic event within 48–72 hours post-surgery.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation: The Classic Signs
content: Dyspnea (73%): Sudden onset shortness of breath.
Pleuritic Chest Pain (66%): Sharp pain on inspiration.
Cough (37%) and Hemoptysis (13%).
Tachypnea (RR > 20/min) and Tachycardia (HR > 100 bpm).
Signs of DVT: Unilateral leg swelling, calf tenderness, erythema.
Syncope: Suggests a massive PE with right heart strain.
Accentuated P2: Sign of pulmonary hypertension.

rows: Crushing pressure, radiation to jaw/arm, ST changes on ECG.
Sudden onset, hyper-resonance, diminished breath sounds.
Sharp pain, pleural rub, often viral or post-inflammatory.
Pain relieved by sitting forward, diffuse ST elevation.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Algorithm
content: Step 1: Clinical Pre-test Probability (Wells Score or Geneva Score).
Step 2: D-Dimer (High sensitivity, low specificity). Only useful to rule out PE in low/moderate risk patients.
Step 3: Imaging - CT Pulmonary Angiogram (CTPA) is the GOLD STANDARD for diagnosis.
Step 4: V/Q Scan - Alternative if CTPA is contraindicated (e.g., Renal failure, severe contrast allergy).
Step 5: Lower Extremity Doppler US - To confirm DVT if PE imaging is inconclusive.
Step 6: Bedside Echocardiography - Check for McConnell's sign (RV free wall akinesia) in unstable patients.

content.explanation: S-wave in Lead I, Q-wave in Lead III, and T-wave inversion in Lead III. Note: Most common ECG finding is actually Sinus Tachycardia.

sections.title: ABG & Lab Findings
content: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG): Respiratory Alkalosis (due to hyperventilation) and Hypoxemia.
A-a Gradient: Usually widened.
Troponin & BNP: Elevated in submassive/massive PE (indicates Right Ventricular strain).
D-Dimer: > 500 ng/mL (using age-adjusted cutoffs if >50 yrs).

rows: Systolic BP < 90 mmHg or 40 mmHg drop from baseline.
Stable BP but evidence of RV dysfunction or Troponin rise.
Hemodynamically stable; no RV strain markers.

sections.title: Acute Management: Anticoagulation
content: LMWH (Enoxaparin): 1 mg/kg SC BID (standard therapeutic dose). Preferred in cancer patients.
Unfractionated Heparin (UFH): IV bolus 80 units/kg, then infusion 18 units/kg/hr. Preferred if thrombolysis or surgery is imminent (reversible).
Fondaparinux: Factor Xa inhibitor, SC daily.
DOACs (Apixaban/Rivaroxaban): Now first-line for stable patients. No bridge needed for Apixaban/Rivaroxaban.
Warfarin: Requires bridging with Heparin for at least 5 days until INR is 2.0-3.0.

sections.title: Emergency Interventions
content: Step 1: Supplemental Oxygen (Maintain Sat >90%).
Step 2: Fluid Resuscitation (Cautious: avoid overloading Right Ventricle).
Step 3: Vasopressors (Norepinephrine) if shock persists.
Step 4: Systemic Thrombolysis (Alteplase 100mg over 2h) for Massive PE.
Step 5: Surgical Embolectomy if thrombolysis is contraindicated or failed.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Crisis
content: Sudden onset Cardiovascular Collapse/Syncope.
Systolic Blood Pressure < 90 mmHg (Obstructive Shock).
New-onset Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB) on ECG.
Refractory Hypoxemia despite 100% FiO2.
Cyanosis of the upper body/neck.

content.explanation: If all 8 are 'NO', PE risk <1%. 1. Age <50, 2. HR <100, 3. O2 Sat >94%, 4. No unilateral leg swelling, 5. No Hemoptysis, 6. No recent surgery/trauma, 7. No prior PE/DVT, 8. No hormone use.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Surgeon
content: Prevention: Early ambulation is the most effective post-op strategy.
Chest X-Ray: Often normal in PE! Look for Westermark Sign (focal oligemia) or Hampton's Hump (wedge-shaped opacity).
PESI Score: Use the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index to decide if a patient can be managed at home.
IVC Filters: Indicated ONLY if there is an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation or recurrent PE despite therapy.

sections.title: Prognosis & Follow-up
sections.content: Untreated PE has a mortality rate of up to 30%. With proper anticoagulation, this drops to <8%. Patients with provoked PE (e.g., post-ophthalmic surgery) generally require 3 months of anticoagulation. Long-term complications include Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension (CTEPH), occurring in 2-4% of survivors; follow-up echocardiography is recommended if dyspnea persists at 3-6 months.
